identity.title: Digital Dice
identity.tagline: Press a button, get a random 1-6 lit up on a 7-segment display — a real die, no dots required.

goal: Build an electronic six-sided die: pressing a button rolls a random number from 1 to 6 and displays it on a 7-segment display, drawn as an actual digit rather than a dot pattern.
simpleSummary: Press a button to roll a random number 1-6, shown on a digit display like a real die.
howItWorks: A 7-segment display is exactly what it sounds like — seven individually-controllable LED bars (plus often a decimal point) arranged to form any digit when the right combination is lit. There's no built-in intelligence in the display itself; every single digit 0-9 is really just a specific pattern of which segments are on and which are off, which is why this project needs a small lookup table mapping each die value to its own array of seven true/false values. The "randomness" comes from Arduino's random() function, and the button-press trigger reuses the exact same edge-detection idea from Push-Button LED Toggle — act once per press, not continuously while held.
toolsNeeded: Arduino IDE (free, installed on your computer)
USB cable to connect the board to your computer
circuitDiagramCaption: Segments A-G on D2-D8 (each through its own resistor); roll button on D9.

wiringSteps.instruction: Identify your display's segment pinout (A through G, plus COM) from its datasheet or the seller's listing.
wiringSteps.detail: 7-segment displays don't have a universal pin arrangement — the physical pin order varies by part, so check yours specifically rather than assuming.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire each segment (A-G) through its own 220Ω resistor to Arduino pins D2 through D8.
wiringSteps.detail: Yes, every single segment needs its own resistor — skipping this to save wiring risks driving each segment LED too hard.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the display's COM pin to GND if it's common-cathode, or to 5V if it's common-anode.
wiringSteps.detail: This one detail changes your code's logic entirely — a common-cathode display lights a segment with HIGH, a common-anode display lights it with LOW. Check which type you have before uploading; the code below assumes common-cathode.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the roll button between D9 and GND, exactly as in Push-Button LED Toggle.
wiringSteps.detail: Same debounced press-detection pattern used throughout the beginner projects.

code.explanation: DIGIT_PATTERNS is the lookup table that does all the real work: showDigit() just looks up the row for the requested value and writes each segment pin HIGH or LOW to match, rather than containing any digit-specific logic itself. randomSeed(analogRead(A0)) reads electrical noise from a floating analog pin to start Arduino's pseudo-random generator differently each power-up — without it, random() would produce the exact same "random" sequence every single time the board resets, which would defeat the whole point of a dice roller.

expectedBehavior: The display shows a starting digit on power-up, and each button press instantly rolls and displays a new random number from 1 to 6.

troubleshooting.issue: Display shows a scrambled or wrong pattern for every number.
troubleshooting.fix: Your display's physical pin order almost certainly doesn't match the SEG_PINS order assumed here — double-check each segment against your specific display's datasheet, not just the pin count.

troubleshooting.issue: Display doesn't light up at all.
troubleshooting.fix: You likely have a common-anode display wired as if it were common-cathode (or vice versa) — try wiring COM to the opposite rail and inverting the HIGH/LOW logic.

troubleshooting.issue: Same number rolls every time after a reset.
troubleshooting.fix: Confirm randomSeed() is being called with a genuinely floating (unconnected) analog pin — a pin that's wired to something will read a consistent value every time, defeating the randomness.

extensions: Add a second 7-segment display and roll two dice at once.
Replace the physical button with a shake-detection trigger using an accelerometer (see MPU6050).
Add a brief "rolling" animation that flashes through a few random digits before settling on the final result.
Extend the lookup table to display all 10 digits (0-9) for a general-purpose number display, not just a die.
